course.title: AP World History: Modern
course.description: Understand the people, ideas, and connections that shaped the world from c. 1200 to the present.
course.previewDescription: Explore how states rose, belief systems spread, trade networks connected regions, and revolutions reshaped societies from c. 1200 to the present.

unit.title: Globalization
unit.description: Study how technology, disease, and environmental change reshaped the world, how the global economy and culture developed, and how people and institutions responded to globalization.

quiz.title: Unit 9 DBQ: Ideas about the role of government
quiz.headline: Ideas about the role of government
quiz.prompt: Evaluate the extent to which ideas about the proper role of government changed in the period 1917–2000.
quiz.instructions: Use at least four documents to support an argument. For at least two documents, explain how the author's point of view, purpose, historical situation, or audience is relevant to your argument. Use at least one piece of specific historical evidence beyond the documents. Include contextualization and develop a complex argument. This is untimed self-assessment practice in AP format.
quiz.note: Original Page One practice. Rubric categories follow the structure of the College Board's AP history rubrics; scoring here is your own self-assessment, not an official score.

rubric.label: Thesis
rubric.guidance: Responds to the prompt with a historically defensible thesis or claim that establishes a line of reasoning.

rubric.label: Contextualization
rubric.guidance: Describes a broader historical context relevant to the prompt.

rubric.label: Evidence from the documents
rubric.guidance: 1 point: accurately describes the content of at least three documents to address the prompt. 2 points: uses the content of at least four documents to support an argument in response to the prompt.

rubric.label: Evidence beyond the documents
rubric.guidance: Uses at least one additional piece of specific historical evidence, not found in the documents, that is relevant to an argument about the prompt.

rubric.label: Sourcing
rubric.guidance: For at least two documents, explains how or why the document's point of view, purpose, historical situation, or audience is relevant to an argument.

rubric.label: Complexity
rubric.guidance: Demonstrates a complex understanding of the topic, using evidence to corroborate, qualify, or modify an argument.

scaffold.label: Read
scaffold.text: Note each document's author, date, and purpose before its content.

scaffold.label: Group
scaffold.text: Sort documents by the claim they support, not by their order.

scaffold.label: Argue
scaffold.text: Use documents as evidence and explain how each supports your claim.

scaffold.label: Source
scaffold.text: Explain why point of view, purpose, situation, or audience matters for two documents.

scaffold.label: Qualify
scaffold.text: Show where the pattern varied by region or social group.

documents.label: “All Power to the Soviets!”
documents.attribution: John Reed, American journalist and socialist who witnessed the Russian Revolution in Petrograd, Ten Days That Shook the World, 1919
documents.content:
In this atmosphere of corruption, of monstrous half-truths, one clear note sounded day after day, the deepening chorus of the Bolsheviki, "All Power to the Soviets! All power to the direct representatives of millions on millions of common workers, soldiers, peasants. Land, bread, an end to the senseless war, an end to secret diplomacy, speculation, treachery. . . . The Revolution is in danger, and with it the cause of the people all over the world!" . . .

Week by week food became scarcer. The daily allowance of bread fell from a pound and a half to a pound, then three quarters, half, and a quarter-pound. Toward the end there was a week without any bread at all.
documents.citation: John Reed, Ten Days That Shook the World (1919), ch. 1. Project Gutenberg eBook #3076.
documents.note: The Bolsheviki were the Bolsheviks, led by Lenin. Soviets were councils of workers and soldiers. The Provisional Government ruled Russia between the tsar's abdication in March 1917 and the Bolshevik seizure of power in November 1917. The ellipsis after “treachery” appears in Reed's own text.
documents.sourceNote: Excerpt text is reused unchanged from Page One's excerpt library, where it is checked against the edition named in the citation.

documents.label: A warning about the peace settlement
documents.attribution: John Maynard Keynes, British economist and Treasury representative at the Paris Peace Conference who resigned in protest in June 1919, The Economic Consequences of the Peace, 1919
documents.content:
This chapter must be one of pessimism. The Treaty includes no provisions for the economic rehabilitation of Europe,--nothing to make the defeated Central Empires into good neighbors, nothing to stabilize the new States of Europe, nothing to reclaim Russia . . . .

If we aim deliberately at the impoverishment of Central Europe, vengeance, I dare predict, will not limp. Nothing can then delay for very long that final civil war between the forces of Reaction and the despairing convulsions of Revolution, before which the horrors of the late German war will fade into nothing . . . .
documents.citation: John Maynard Keynes, The Economic Consequences of the Peace (New York: Harcourt, Brace and Howe, 1920), chs. 6–7. Project Gutenberg eBook #15776.
documents.note: The Central Empires were Germany and Austria-Hungary. “The late German war” is the First World War.
documents.sourceNote: Excerpt text is reused unchanged from Page One's excerpt library, where it is checked against the edition named in the citation.

documents.label: Democracy and communism
documents.attribution: Harry S. Truman, president of the United States, inaugural address, January 20, 1949
documents.content:
That regime adheres to a false philosophy which purports to offer freedom, security, and greater opportunity to mankind. Misled by this philosophy, many peoples have sacrificed their liberties only to learn to their sorrow that deceit and mockery, poverty and tyranny, are their reward.

That false philosophy is communism.

Communism is based on the belief that man is so weak and inadequate that he is unable to govern himself, and therefore requires the rule of strong masters.

Democracy is based on the conviction that man has the moral and intellectual capacity, as well as the inalienable right, to govern himself with reason and justice. . . .

Communism holds that the world is so deeply divided into opposing classes that war is inevitable.

Democracy holds that free nations can settle differences justly and maintain lasting peace.
documents.citation: Harry S. Truman, Inaugural Address, January 20, 1949. Text checked against the C-SPAN transcript in the NLTK corpus (inaugural/1949-Truman.txt).
documents.note: “That regime” is the government of the Soviet Union. Truman spoke two years after announcing aid to Greece and Turkey and while the Berlin airlift was still under way.
documents.sourceNote: Excerpt text is reused unchanged from Page One's excerpt library, where it is checked against the edition named in the citation.

documents.label: A call for environmental regulation
documents.attribution: Richard Nixon, president of the United States, State of the Union address to Congress, January 22, 1970
documents.content:
The great question of the seventies is, shall we surrender to our surroundings, or shall we make our peace with nature and begin to make reparations for the damage we have done to our air, to our land, and to our water? . . .

We still think of air as free. But clean air is not free, and neither is clean water. The price tag on pollution control is high. Through our years of past carelessness we incurred a debt to nature, and now that debt is being called. . . .

We can no longer afford to consider air and water common property, free to be abused by anyone without regard to the consequences. . . . This requires comprehensive new regulations. It also requires that, to the extent possible, the price of goods should be made to include the costs of producing and disposing of them without damage to the environment.
documents.citation: Richard Nixon, Annual Message to the Congress on the State of the Union, January 22, 1970. Text checked against the C-SPAN transcript in the NLTK corpus (state_union/1970-Nixon.txt, converted to UTF-8).
documents.note: Three months later, millions of Americans took part in the first Earth Day, and in December 1970 the federal Environmental Protection Agency began work.
documents.sourceNote: Excerpt text is reused unchanged from Page One's excerpt library, where it is checked against the edition named in the citation.

documents.label: “Government is not the solution”
documents.attribution: Ronald Reagan, president of the United States, inaugural address, January 20, 1981
documents.content:
These United States are confronted with an economic affliction of great proportions. We suffer from the longest and one of the worst sustained inflations in our national history. . . .

But great as our tax burden is, it has not kept pace with public spending. For decades, we have piled deficit upon deficit, mortgaging our future and our children's future for the temporary convenience of the present. . . .

In this present crisis, government is not the solution to our problem . . . .

In the days ahead I will propose removing the roadblocks that have slowed our economy and reduced productivity.
documents.citation: Ronald Reagan, Inaugural Address, January 20, 1981. Text checked against the C-SPAN transcript in the NLTK corpus (inaugural/1981-Reagan.txt).
documents.note: The transcript used to check this excerpt ends the third paragraph's sentence at “problem”; as delivered, Reagan continued, “government is the problem.” In 1980, US inflation was above 12 percent.
documents.sourceNote: Excerpt text is reused unchanged from Page One's excerpt library, where it is checked against the edition named in the citation.

documents.label: The Revolution of 1989
documents.attribution: George H. W. Bush, president of the United States, State of the Union address to Congress, January 31, 1990
documents.content:
The events of the year just ended, the Revolution of '89, have been a chain reaction, changes so striking that it marks the beginning of a new era in the world's affairs. . . .

A year ago in Poland, Lech Walesa declared that he was ready to open a dialog with the Communist rulers of that country; and today, with the future of a free Poland in their own hands, members of Solidarity lead the Polish Government.

A year ago, freedom's playwright, Vaclav Havel, languished as a prisoner in Prague. And today it's Vaclav Havel, President of Czechoslovakia.

And 1 year ago, Erich Honecker of East Germany claimed history as his guide, and he predicted the Berlin Wall would last another hundred years. And today, less than 1 year later, it's the Wall that's history.
documents.citation: George H. W. Bush, Address on the State of the Union, January 31, 1990. Text checked against the C-SPAN transcript in the NLTK corpus (state_union/1990-Bush.txt).
documents.note: Names appear as printed in the transcript, without diacritical marks: Lech Wałęsa led the Polish trade union Solidarity, and Václav Havel was a dissident Czech playwright. Erich Honecker led East Germany until October 1989.
documents.sourceNote: Excerpt text is reused unchanged from Page One's excerpt library, where it is checked against the edition named in the citation.

documents.label: Globalization and rules for trade
documents.attribution: Bill Clinton, president of the United States, State of the Union address to Congress, January 27, 2000
documents.content:
To realize the full possibilities of this economy, we must reach beyond our own borders, to shape the revolution that is tearing down barriers and building new networks among nations and individuals and economies and cultures: globalization. It's the central reality of our time.

Of course, change this profound is both liberating and threatening to people. But there's no turning back. . . .

The first thing we have got to do is to forge a new consensus on trade. Now, those of us who believe passionately in the power of open trade, we have to ensure that it lifts both our living standards and our values, never tolerating abusive child labor or a race to the bottom in the environment and worker protection. But others must recognize that open markets and rule-based trade are the best engines we know of for raising living standards, reducing global poverty and environmental destruction, and assuring the free flow of ideas.
documents.citation: William J. Clinton, Address Before a Joint Session of the Congress on the State of the Union, January 27, 2000. Text checked against the C-SPAN transcript in the NLTK corpus (state_union/2000-Clinton.txt).
documents.note: Two months earlier, tens of thousands of protesters had disrupted a World Trade Organization meeting in Seattle.

quiz.modelResponse:
In 1900, most governments played a limited role in daily economic life, but the First World War, the Russian Revolution, and the Great Depression led many people to ask whether governments should take on much more. The Cold War then divided the world between states with market economies and states with planned economies, and the late twentieth century produced new debates about markets and regulation.

Between 1917 and 2000, ideas about the role of government changed substantially, moving from confidence in an active state in the early and middle decades toward greater trust in markets after 1980, but the shift was incomplete because governments continued to regulate, to set rules for trade, and to defend political systems.

In the first half of the century, many writers expected governments to act. In Petrograd, the Bolsheviks called for "All Power to the Soviets" and promised land, bread, and peace as the Provisional Government failed to feed the city (Document 1). John Reed, an American socialist who supported the revolution, had reason to highlight the Bolsheviks' appeal, but his description of falling bread rations helps explain why many Russians turned to a government that promised to take control of the economy. After the war, Keynes warned that the Treaty of Versailles had "no provisions for the economic rehabilitation of Europe" and predicted revolution if Central Europe were impoverished (Document 2). Writing after resigning from the British delegation, Keynes wanted to persuade readers that governments had a responsibility to plan for recovery. The Great Depression and the New Deal in the United States confirmed this view: governments took on responsibility for employment and relief.

During the Cold War, the debate was about which kind of government should rule. President Truman described communism as based on the belief that people need "strong masters," while democracy rested on the "capacity . . . to govern himself" (Document 3). Speaking in 1949 during the Berlin airlift, Truman had a purpose of rallying Americans and allies behind containment, so his contrast is stark. Yet he did not oppose government action: the Marshall Plan committed billions of dollars in public aid to rebuild Western Europe. Nixon's 1970 call for "comprehensive new regulations" on pollution (Document 4) shows that active government remained a mainstream view in a Republican administration, and he used it to respond to growing public concern and the creation of the Environmental Protection Agency.

After 1975, confidence in the state declined. Reagan said that "government is not the solution to our problem" and proposed to remove "roadblocks" to the economy (Document 5). He spoke after a decade of inflation and slow growth, and his inaugural address was meant to justify tax cuts and deregulation. Similar ideas shaped Margaret Thatcher's privatizations in Britain and the market reforms of Deng Xiaoping in China. The collapse of communist governments in 1989, celebrated by Bush (Document 6), seemed to confirm the failure of central planning, though Bush was also claiming credit for his country's Cold War policy. Gorbachev's perestroika and glasnost had opened the way.

By 2000, the debate had shifted again. Clinton described globalization as "the central reality of our time" and urged "rule-based trade" that would not tolerate "a race to the bottom" in the environment and worker protection (Document 7). Speaking soon after the protests at the WTO meeting in Seattle, he had a political reason to show that he took critics seriously. His position shows that even leaders who praised markets accepted a role for government in setting rules.

In conclusion, ideas about government moved from confidence in state direction to greater trust in markets, but governments never stopped regulating, protecting, and setting the terms of exchange, so the change was real but incomplete.

modelNotes.label: Contextualization
modelNotes.text: The first paragraph describes the role of governments before 1917, the effects of the world wars and the Depression, and the Cold War division.

modelNotes.label: Thesis
modelNotes.text: The thesis answers the question of extent and previews a pattern of change with limits.

modelNotes.label: Evidence from the documents
modelNotes.text: All seven documents are used as evidence, grouped by period.

modelNotes.label: Evidence beyond the documents
modelNotes.text: The New Deal, the Marshall Plan, the Environmental Protection Agency, Thatcher's privatizations, Deng Xiaoping's reforms, and Gorbachev's reforms are specific evidence not found in the documents.

modelNotes.label: Sourcing
modelNotes.text: The essay explains Reed's sympathies, Keynes's purpose after resigning, Truman's Cold War audience, Reagan's response to inflation, Bush's claim to credit, and Clinton's political situation after the Seattle protests.

modelNotes.label: Complexity
modelNotes.text: The essay qualifies the claim of a shift toward markets by showing continuing regulation in Nixon's and Clinton's addresses and by noting that Bush and Truman were also political speakers.

quiz.alternateModel: A different strong essay could argue that the central change was not the size of government but its purpose, grouping Documents 1–3 as arguments about which political system should rule and Documents 4–7 as arguments about how far markets should be regulated.
commonErrors: Treating the documents, most of which are by American presidents, as evidence for the whole world.
Summarizing each document in order instead of grouping them by claim.
Claiming that government's role simply grew or simply shrank throughout the century.
Quoting speeches without noting that political speakers have purposes and audiences.
